plot_or_argument: Black August sets the Communist revolution of the 1940s against the band of friends who resist it - the arrested England, the escape, the underground - in the thriller form of Wheatley's dystopia of the decade's politics.
narrative_structure: A dystopian thriller in the chapters of the revolution and the escape. A novel cast as the document, diary or confession of a subject inside the system, the invented vocabulary of the state carrying the satire. A novel of pursuit and escape in chapters, each carrying a set piece of travel, combat or discovery.
principal_characters: the band of friends; the revolutionaries; the arrested England
meter_and_prosody: Prose. Prose of the anti-utopia: the document, the diary or the confession of a subject inside the system, the invented vocabulary of the state, and the satiric inversion of the utopian description. The author's characteristic manner is the thriller's pace and the set piece of the escape.
historical_context: An England of the near future under revolution. The record dates the work as composed in 1934 and first published in 1934 and it is catalogued under dystopian fiction and the anti-utopian satire; imperial adventure romance.
literary_significance: Black August is Wheatley's dystopia: it joined the anti-Utopian novel to the popular thriller and made the revolution in England the matter of the between-wars bestseller.
attribution_notes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Dennis Yates Wheatley. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as secondary canon.
bibliographical_notes: First published in 1934, as novel (the dystopian thriller), by Dennis Wheatley. Composed in 1934. The record grades the work as secondary canon.

title: The Devil Rides Out
description: The occult thriller of the black mass and the devil's ride. It is a verse work of 1935 by Dennis Wheatley; it belongs to The Ghost Story and the Modern Weird Tale and it is catalogued here under ghost story and the modern weird tale; detective novel and the golden age mystery and the record grades it as major canon.
plot_or_argument: The Devil Rides Out sets the Duke de Richleau against the Satanist Mocata for the soul of the young Simon Aron, through the black mass, the ritual circle and the night of the chase, in the occult thriller whose ritual detail made it the classic of the English devil novel.
narrative_structure: An occult thriller in the chapters of the ritual and the chase. A short narrative built on the antiquarian's document or object, with the haunting approached by stages and never fully explained.
principal_characters: the Duke de Richleau; Mocata, the Satanist; Simon Aron; the rescued
meter_and_prosody: Verse. Prose of the weird tale: the antiquarian or scholarly narrator, the document or the object that carries the haunting, the exact topography, and the refusal of a natural explanation. The author's characteristic manner is the thriller's pace and the set piece of the escape.
historical_context: England in the mid-1930s. The record dates the work as composed between 1934 and 1935 and first published in 1935 and the corpus places it within The Ghost Story and the Modern Weird Tale, it is catalogued under ghost story and the modern weird tale; detective novel and the golden age mystery.
literary_significance: The Devil Rides Out is Wheatley's classic: its black mass, its ritual circle and its Mocata made the occult thriller a national fashion and remain the standard of the English devil novel.
attribution_notes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Dennis Yates Wheatley. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.
bibliographical_notes: First published in 1935, as novel (the occult thriller), by Dennis Wheatley. Composed between 1934 and 1935. The record grades the work as major canon.

title: O Absalom!
description: The national bestseller of the Welsh preacher and his son. It is a prose fiction work of 1934 by Howard Spring; it is catalogued here under novel of development and the growth story; regional novel and the american local-colour inheritance and the record grades it as major canon.
plot_or_argument: O Absalom! tells the rise of the Welsh preacher Arnold Ryrie and the quarrel with the son who is destroyed by the father's career, in the plain parable prose of the bestseller that made Spring's name.
narrative_structure: A parable novel in the chapters of the calling and the quarrel. A novel in chapters grouped by the stages of a life, from childhood through the education and the first disappointments to the settlement of the adult. A novel in chapters inside one region, the seasons, the trades and the dialect carrying the plot.
principal_characters: Arnold Ryrie, the preacher; the son; the Welsh chapel household
literary_form: Novel (the Welsh parable); novel of development
meter_and_prosody: Prose. Prose fiction of formation: the narrative follows one consciousness from childhood or youth to settlement, in chapters grouped by the stages of the life, with the earlier manner recalled and judged by the later. The author's characteristic manner is the Welsh pulpit and the household of the preacher.
historical_context: Wales and the Welsh pulpit in the early twentieth century. The record dates the work as composed between 1933 and 1934 and first published in 1934 and it is catalogued under novel of development and the growth story; regional novel and the american local-colour inheritance.
literary_significance: O Absalom! was one of the great bestsellers of the 1930s: its preacher, its son and its parable of the calling made the Welsh pulpit the matter of the popular novel.
attribution_notes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Howard Spring. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.
bibliographical_notes: First published in 1934, as novel (the welsh parable), by Howard Spring. Composed between 1933 and 1934. The record grades the work as major canon.

title: My Son, My Son!
description: The sequel parable of the son and the calling. It is a prose fiction work of 1938 by Howard Spring; it is catalogued here under novel of development and the growth story; realist novel of common life.
plot_or_argument: My Son, My Son! carries Spring's parable into the modern city, following the son of the wealthy house through the business, the marriage and the ruin, in the same plain moral prose of the bestseller.
narrative_structure: A parable novel of the business and the family. A novel in chapters grouped by the stages of a life, from childhood through the education and the first disappointments to the settlement of the adult. A novel in chapters, the action carried in sequence from the opening situation to the closing resolution, with the material world of the household described at length.
principal_characters: the son of the house; the father; the wife and the business
meter_and_prosody: Prose. Prose fiction of formation: the narrative follows one consciousness from childhood or youth to settlement, in chapters grouped by the stages of the life, with the earlier manner recalled and judged by the later. The author's characteristic manner is the Welsh pulpit and the household of the preacher.
historical_context: The English city of the late 1930s. The record dates the work as composed between 1937 and 1938 and first published in 1938 and it is catalogued under novel of development and the growth story; realist novel of common life.
literary_significance: My Son, My Son! continued the O Absalom! parable into the city and confirmed Spring as the moral novelist of the between-wars bestseller.

title: Fame Is the Spur
description: The political novel of the radical career and its price. It is a prose fiction work of 1940 by Howard Spring; it is catalogued here under condition-of-england novel and the edwardian social panorama; novel of development and the growth story and the record grades it as major canon.
plot_or_argument: Fame Is the Spur follows Hamer Shawcross from the Welsh radical beginnings through the Liberal career and the betrayals of the ideal to the peerage and the ruin of the son, in the political prose of the career novel that reads the decade's politics through one man's rise.
narrative_structure: A career novel in the chapters of the rise and the price. A novel in chapters of survey, the household and the institution described as types of the whole society, the argument carried by contrast between scenes. A novel in chapters grouped by the stages of a life, from childhood through the education and the first disappointments to the settlement of the adult.
principal_characters: Hamer Shawcross, the radical; the wife; the son; the party
meter_and_prosody: Prose. Prose of the social panorama: the long sentence of survey, the household and the institution described as types of the whole society, and the argument carried by contrast between scenes rather than by authorial comment. The author's characteristic manner is the Welsh pulpit and the household of the preacher.
historical_context: Wales and Westminster from the 1890s to the 1930s. The record dates the work as composed between 1939 and 1940 and first published in 1940 and it is catalogued under condition-of-england novel and the edwardian social panorama; novel of development and the growth story.
literary_significance: Fame Is the Spur is Spring's political novel: its Shawcross - the radical made lord - is the classic study of the corrupted ideal in the popular political fiction of the war years.
